title: Family Law Amendment (Family Violence and Cross-examination of Parties) Bill 2018
short_title: Family Law Amendment (Family Violence and Cross-examination of Parties) Bill 2018

divisions.question: Family Law Amendment (Family Violence and Cross-Examination of Parties) Bill 2018 - Second Reading - Access to legal representation

speeches.speaker: Christian Porter
speeches.brief: The Family Law Amendment (Family Violence and Cross-examination of Parties) Bill 2018 was moved, banning perpetrators of family violence from directly cross-examining their victims in all family law proceedings, with cross-examination to be conducted by a legal representative. The bill responds to a 2016 COAG recommendation and a 2017 House committee report, citing that 1 in 6 Australian women and 1 in 16 men have experienced partner violence, and that direct cross-examination occurred in 173 family violence matters between 2015 and 2017.

speeches.speaker: Sarah Henderson
speeches.brief: The Turnbull government introduced the Family Law Amendment (Family Violence and Cross-examination of Parties) Bill to prohibit perpetrators of family violence from directly cross-examining victims in family law proceedings, with the prohibition applying where convictions, charges or final family violence orders exist. The government also committed $54.4 million in the 2018 budget for violence-affected women's services, including $11.5 million for 1800RESPECT and $14.2 million for the Office of the eSafety Commissioner.

speeches.speaker: Mark Dreyfus
speeches.brief: Labor supported the Family Law Amendment (Family Violence and Cross-examination of Parties) Bill 2018, which imposes an automatic ban on direct cross-examination of family violence survivors by perpetrators, but moved an amendment calling for additional funding for Legal Aid, noting that 173 survivors were directly cross-examined over two years and that the government's own senate committee recommended funding details be made public before the bill's Senate debate. Labor had previously pledged $43 million for legal aid to support the ban.

speeches.speaker: Bert Van Manen
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the Family Law Amendment (Family Violence and Cross-examination of Parties) Bill 2018, which prohibits alleged perpetrators of family violence from personally cross-examining their victims in family law proceedings, citing a $26 billion annual cost of violence against women and the need to prevent retraumatisation.

speeches.speaker: Graham Perrett
speeches.brief: The speaker welcomed the bill banning direct cross-examination of alleged family violence victims but argued it would be useless without funding, noting Labor's 2016 policy included $43.2 million for full legal representation. The speaker also criticized the government for failing to allocate funding and for not consulting stakeholders on broader family law reforms.

speeches.speaker: Christopher Pyne
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that moving a suspension of standing orders by merely mentioning the Family Law Amendment (Family Violence and Cross-examination of Parties) Bill 2018 would set a dangerous precedent, allowing interruptions to substantive debates on any bill.

speeches.speaker: Russell Broadbent
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the Family Law Amendment (Family Violence and Cross-examination of Parties) Bill 2018, arguing it removes the threat of direct cross-examination of victims by alleged perpetrators in family law matters. They noted the Senate Legal and Constitutional Affairs Committee recommended passage subject to public funding details, and called for future monitoring of the legislation's effectiveness.

speeches.speaker: Sharon Claydon
speeches.brief: The speaker supported an amendment to guarantee additional legal aid funding for the Family Law Amendment (Family Violence and Cross-examination of Parties) Bill 2018, which prohibits perpetrators from cross-examining victims, and noted that 46 Australian women have been killed by violence in the first 36 weeks of the year.

speeches.speaker: Chris Crewther
speeches.brief: The Family Law Amendment (Family Violence and Cross-examination of Parties) Bill 2018 prohibits personal cross-examination of victims by alleged perpetrators in family law proceedings where family violence is alleged, with automatic bans under specified conditions and court discretion otherwise, and requires legal representation and other protective measures.

speeches.speaker: Shayne Neumann
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the Family Law Amendment (Family Violence and Cross-Examination of Parties) Bill 2018 should ban perpetrators from directly cross-examining victims in family law proceedings, citing trauma and power imbalances. They called on the government to match Labor’s $43 million commitment to fund legal aid for the ban, noting that 72% of cases involve direct cross-examination and court delays have worsened, with median trial times rising to 17 months in the Family Court and 15.2 months in the Federal Circuit Court.

speeches.speaker: Chris Hayes
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the bill banning direct cross-examination of domestic violence victims by perpetrators in family law hearings, but argued it is flawed because it includes no additional funding for legal aid, unlike Labor's previous $43 million commitment, warning this could cause court delays and injustice.

speeches.speaker: Cathy O'Toole
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the Family Law Amendment (Family Violence and Cross-examination of Parties) Bill 2018 must pass to stop perpetrators cross-examining domestic violence survivors, and stressed that additional funding—specifically Labor’s promised $43 million for Legal Aid—is urgently needed to support the bill’s implementation, criticising the government for not matching this commitment.

speeches.speaker: Emma Husar
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the Family Law Amendment Bill must be matched with $43 million in legal aid funding to end the practice of domestic violence survivors being cross-examined by their perpetrators in court, calling the current situation "shameful" and a failure of the government. They cited 1,068 domestic assaults in their community over 12 months and noted that 56 women and 95 children were turned away from shelters in a single month due to underfunding.

speeches.speaker: Linda Burney
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the bill banning direct cross-examination of domestic violence survivors by their abusers is necessary but will fail without additional funding, noting Labor's $43 million commitment to legal aid and criticising the government for refusing similar funding.

speeches.speaker: Jason Wood
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the Family Law Amendment (Family Violence and Cross-examination of Parties) Bill 2018 is important legislation to protect victims from being personally cross-examined by perpetrators in family violence cases, citing personal experiences as a former police officer and noting that one in five families in his electorate of La Trobe experiences family violence. He fully supported the bill, which prohibits personal cross-examination when there are convictions, charges, or orders involving violence, and acknowledged bipartisan support.

speeches.speaker: Craig Kelly
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the Family Law Amendment (Family Violence and Cross-examination of Parties) Bill 2018, citing stories of clients facing legal bills up to $800,000 and arguing that perpetrators of family violence should be prevented from cross-examining their victims.

speeches.speaker: Christian Porter
speeches.brief: The government argued the Family Law Amendment (Family Violence and Cross-examination of Parties) Bill 2018 protects victims from being cross-examined by their perpetrator, and committed to announcing adequate Legal Aid funding details before Senate debate. The government opposed Labor's amendment as unnecessary delay, agreeing to all Senate committee recommendations.
